options.text: A rock containing enough metal to make extraction worthwhile
options.explanation: The worth-threshold idea is the definition: the rock must pay for the extraction process.

options.text: Any rock found deep underground
options.explanation: Depth is irrelevant; what matters is the metal content being high enough to extract.

options.text: A pure metal nugget dug from the ground
options.explanation: A nugget of uncombined metal needs no extraction, so it is not what the word ore describes.
options.misconception: native metal mistaken for an ore

options.text: The waste rock left after a metal is removed
options.explanation: That describes spoil or tailings; an ore is the metal-rich rock before extraction.

questions.stem: Why is extracting a metal from an oxide ore called a reduction process?

options.text: Because oxygen is removed from the metal compound
options.explanation: Loss of oxygen is the definition of reduction in oxygen language, which is exactly what extraction does to an oxide ore.

options.text: Because the amount of metal gets smaller
options.explanation: The metal is gained, not lost; the name refers to oxygen removal, not to quantity.

options.text: Because the furnace temperature is lowered
options.explanation: Blast furnaces run hot; the chemical meaning of reduction has nothing to do with cooling.

options.text: Because electrons are gained by oxygen
options.explanation: In oxygen language the defining event is oxygen leaving the metal compound.
options.misconception: electron wording attached to the wrong species

questions.stem: Haematite is the ore of which metal?

options.text: Iron
options.explanation: Haematite is iron oxide, the ore fed into the blast furnace to make iron.

options.text: Aluminium
options.explanation: Aluminium's ore is bauxite, which contains aluminium oxide.

options.text: Copper
options.explanation: Copper appears in the crust as compounds too, but haematite is specifically the iron ore.

options.text: Gold
options.explanation: Gold is unreactive and is found as the element, so it has no ore to name.

questions.stem: Which three routes are named for getting a metal out of its ore?

options.text: Electrolysis, a blast furnace, or reaction with a more reactive material
options.explanation: These are exactly the three processes listed for extraction, chosen according to the metal's reactivity.

options.text: Filtration, distillation and crystallisation
options.explanation: Those are separation techniques for mixtures; extraction needs chemistry that removes oxygen or uses electricity.

options.text: Dissolving, filtering and evaporating
options.explanation: These physical steps cannot reduce an oxide ore to the metal on their own.
options.misconception: physical processing confused with reduction chemistry

options.text: Mining, crushing and sorting
options.explanation: These prepare the rock but do not release the metal from its compounds.
options.misconception: physical processing confused with reduction chemistry

questions.stem: Bauxite is an ore of which metal, and what kind of compound is it?

options.text: Aluminium, occurring as its oxide
options.explanation: Bauxite is aluminium oxide, which is why aluminium extraction removes oxygen by electrolysis.

options.text: Iron, occurring as its carbonate
options.explanation: Iron's ore haematite is an oxide, and bauxite belongs to aluminium, not iron.

options.text: Aluminium, occurring as the free metal
options.explanation: Aluminium is reactive, so it is locked in compounds; bauxite is its oxide ore.

options.text: Copper, occurring as its sulfate
options.explanation: Neither the metal nor the compound type matches; bauxite is aluminium oxide.

questions.stem: Which pair of metals is typically found as the uncombined element?

options.text: Gold and platinum
options.explanation: Both are chemically stable enough to exist as elements in the crust and can be mined directly.

options.text: Iron and aluminium
options.explanation: Both are reactive enough to need extraction from their oxide ores, haematite and bauxite.

options.text: Sodium and potassium
options.explanation: These are among the most reactive metals and exist only in compounds.

options.text: Zinc and copper
options.explanation: These metals are extracted from ores, so they do not occur usefully as elements.

questions.stem: Why do unreactive metals occur as elements rather than compounds?

options.text: Their chemical stability means they do not easily react with other substances
options.explanation: Without easy reaction there is nothing to convert them into compounds, so they remain uncombined.

options.text: They are too dense to form compounds
options.explanation: Density plays no part in compound formation; reactivity does.
options.misconception: physical property given a chemical role

options.text: They were only discovered after ores were used up
options.explanation: Occurrence is set by chemistry, not by history or supply.

options.text: The crust is too cold for them to react
options.explanation: Temperature is not the deciding factor; the metals simply have little tendency to react.

questions.stem: A metal M can reduce the oxide of metal N only if which condition holds?

options.text: M is more reactive than N
options.explanation: Only the more reactive metal can take oxygen away from the compound of a less reactive one.

options.text: M is less reactive than N
options.explanation: The less reactive metal cannot wrest oxygen from a more reactive metal's compound.

options.text: M and N have equal reactivity
options.explanation: Equal reactivity gives no driving force for the oxygen to move.

options.text: N is above hydrogen in the reactivity series
options.explanation: The comparison that matters is between M and N themselves, not their position against hydrogen.
options.misconception: wrong reference point for the comparison

questions.stem: Why does gold need neither a blast furnace nor electrolysis to be obtained?

options.text: It already exists as the element, so there is no compound to break down
options.explanation: Extraction processes exist to release metals from compounds; gold is found uncombined, so no such step is needed.

options.text: Because gold is too valuable to process industrially
options.explanation: Value is irrelevant; the chemistry is what removes the need for extraction.

options.text: Because gold melts at room temperature
options.explanation: Gold is solid at room temperature, and melting would not release it from a compound anyway.

options.text: Because gold is lighter than the rock around it
options.explanation: Density may help panning but it is not why no chemical extraction is required.
options.misconception: physical separation confused with chemical extraction

questions.stem: Most metals are extracted from ores, but which group is the exception?

options.text: The unreactive metals, often found as the uncombined element
options.explanation: The rule covers most metals; the exception is the chemically stable few found as elements.

options.text: The most reactive metals, which refuse to form compounds
options.explanation: The most reactive metals form compounds most readily and always need extraction.

options.text: The transition metals, which are always native
options.explanation: Many transition metals, such as iron and copper, are extracted from ores.
options.misconception: blanket claim about a metal family

options.text: No exceptions exist; every metal needs extraction
options.explanation: Gold and platinum are clear exceptions found as the element.
